The main point is that the volume in the ventricles DOES NOT change even though the intraventricular pressure rapidly increases. input: Given question: Sally has recently been experiencing a burning pain behind her sternum which is worse after eating and when lying down. After some of her own internet research she has decided to purchase some over the counter Gaviscon. She finds that this has helped relieve her symptoms, but the problem doesn't go away.  She goes to the GP, who diagnoses her with GORD and prescribes her omeprazole.  The GP tells her to stop taking the Gaviscon. Why is this? Option A: The internet is not an accurate source of medical advice. Gaviscon actually worsens the effects of GORD. Option B: Gaviscon is an enzyme inducer, therefore accelerating the metabolism of omeprazole. Option C: Omeprazole is a more effective drug, so there is no point taking Gaviscon as well. Option D: Omeprazole requires the acid environment of the stomach to be activated. The correct answer is Option D.
reference: Gaviscon is an antacid which may be effective for mild reflux. Omeprazole is a PPI which is more effective than antacids. PPIs are prodrugs, which means they are initially inactive. They require to acid environment of the stomach to be converted to a pharmacologically active form.
best_explanation:
Gaviscon is an antacid, which neutralises gastric acid. Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor, which stops the stomach producing gastric acid. As omeprazole is more effective, Sally doesn't need to take both. When taking omeprazole, the stomach should be kept acidic to activate the drug. Gaviscon, being an antacid, would neutralise the acidic environment required for omeprazole activation. Therefore the GP has told her to stop taking the Gaviscon. reference: A is the correct answer.The role of RANK-L in bone healing is to regulate differentiation, activation + survival. Bone healing: 1. Haematoma: tearing of blood vessels -> local bleeding. Pro-inflammatory cytokines released, activating cells of the immune system to remove damaged tissues + further secretion of VEGF to stimulate healing.2. Inflammation: macrophages invade the clot + start destruction, followed by vascular ingrowth. 3. Granulation/fibrocartilaginous callus: VEGF stimulates angiogenesis. This occurs in the presence of fibroblasts + mesenchymal cells (stimulated by bone morphogenetic proteins). Chondrogenesis begins, laying down collagen-rich fibrocartilaginous network to replace blood clot. Osteoprogenitor cells begin laying woven bone adjacent to periosteal layers.4. Bony callus formation: RANK-L active. Cartilaginous callus begins endochondral ossification, resorption of cartilage matrix + calcification. Mesenchymal cells continue to migrate as blood vessels continue to proliferate.5. Consolidation: Callus calcifies + ends unite w/ bony callus. Chondrocytes undergo terminal differentiation + become apoptotic.6. Remodelling: woven bone is replaced w/ lamellar bone + excess bone resorbed. Takes years + is often incomplete. Influenced by Wolff’s law and Piezoelectric charges.

instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: A patient has been rushed into the emergency ER after suffering a stroke. The neurologist discovers they have lesions in the left S1 and S2 cortices of the brain. When the patient wakes up, the doctor runs some tests including a test that involves pinching the patient. The doctor finds that the patient is experiencing less pain on the right side of the body and struggles to identify the location where they were pinched. Why is this? Option A: The stroke has led to damage of the spinothalamic tract Option B: The stroke has led to damage of the lateral pain system Option C: The patient has a lower perception of pain Option D: The stroke has led to damage medial pain system Option E: The stroke has led to damage of the dorsal column medial leminiscus tract The correct answer is Option B.
reference: B: The lateral pain system is found in the cortex and can be damaged by lesions of the cortices. This system is involved in mediating pain perception (mediates the perception of the sensory and discriminative aspect of pain, such as being able to tell where someone has pinched you). Damage to this system may result in patients perceiving less pain and inability to discriminate where pain has come from. A: Spinothalamic tract is an ascending tract and is involved in transmitting pain stimuli. However, it is not at a risk of being damaged by lesions of the cortices. Damage would have to occur lower down for this to be a potential answer.  C: This answer is technically correct, however can be a result of multiple factors and is not the single best answer. Question B is more thorough.  D: The medial pain system is involved in the processing of pain via affective (state of mind i.e. fight or flight) and cognitive- evaluation (the meaning of pain, i.e. why soldiers may perceive less pain than civilians because pain has the positive meaning that they are still alive). It is not involved in sensory and discriminative aspect of pain.  E: The Dorsal column medial leminiscus tract is an ascending tract for vibrations, discriminitive touch and proprioception. It is unlikely to be affected by lesions of the cortices and even if it was, it is not involved in pain or noxious stimuli transmission. See Case 1: Psychology of Acute pain and Analgesia 1 by Dr. Thanasi Hassoulas​
best_explanation: The lateral pain system is responsible for the conscious perception of pain. It is mediated by the spinothalamic tract. The spinothalamic tract is damaged in this case so the patient struggles to identify the location of pain. The patient still experiences pain due to the medial pain system being intact. The medial pain system is responsible for the emotional aspect of pain.  Source: PCS 3 Neuroanatomy of Pain lecture.  Case 1 Phantom Pain lecture.

input: Given question: Our immunity can be divided into that which is Innate and that which is Adaptive, each comprising of different cell types, with different functions. Which cell type "bridges the gap" between the two types of immune response? Have a think about how it does this. Option A: Mast Cell Option B: Macrophage Option C: Neutrophil Option D: Dendritic Cell Option E: Natural Killer Cell The correct answer is Option D.
reference: Dendritic Cells bridge the gap between the innate and adaptive immune response.  They are very similar to macrophages in that they are capable of Phagocytosis, Antigen presentation, PAMP recognition and Cytokine release. The fundamental difference is that dendritic cells are also motile, meaning they can migrate to the draining lymph nodes in order to deliver components of pathogens (antigen presentation) to activate the B and T cells of the adaptive immune response.
best_explanation: The dendritic cell is the link between innate and adaptive immunity. It has a key role in the bridging of the two. It is capable of both innate and adaptive responses to pathogens. It has PRR (pathogen recognition receptors) on its surface to recognise and respond to pathogens, and also the ability to process and present antigens to T and B cells, thereby activating an adaptive immune response.  Mast cells, macrophages, neutrophils and natural killer cells are all associated with the innate immune response. Mast cells release histamine, important in parasitic infections. Macrophages have a role in phagocytosis and are important in the early stages of infection. Neutrophils have a vital role in combating pathogens in the early stages of infection. input: Given question: A patient enters a GP surgery having hit her elbow on a banister whilst walking down the stairs. When making a fist, only her pinky and ring finger are able to bend. What nerve has the patient damaged? Option A: Ulnar Option B: Median Option C: Radial Option D: Musculocutaneous Option E: Axillary The correct answer is Option B.
reference: The condition is known as the "sign of benediction", and is caused when the median nerve is damaged at the wrist or elbow.
best_explanation: The Median nerve innervates the flexors of the forearm. The ulnar nerve innervates the flexor of the hand. The radial nerve innervates the extensors of the forearm and the musculocutaneous nerve innervates the lateral aspect of the forearm. The axillary nerve innervates the deltoid and teres minor.  Damage to the median nerve will cause flexed 4th and 5th digits along with the thumb.  Damage to the ulnar nerve will cause flexed 4th and 5th digits along with the thumb. input: Given question: Mr Vallance is having his tooth extracted. It is decided he needs a local anaesthetic which inhibits fast-gated sodium channels. Which one of the following medications is suitable? Option A: Diazepam Option B: Propofol Option C: Amobarbital Option D: Lignocaine Option E: Nitrous oxide The correct answer is Option D.
reference: Correct answer is lignocaine. We learnt about lignocaine and tetracaine in the autonomic nervous system lecture in PCS 3. Propofol and Amobarbital - both intravenous general anaesthetics Diazepam - sedative, can be intravenous or in tablet form Nitrous oxide - a common recreational drug amongst reckless youngsters who leave the cannisters all over the street, this is also known as laughing gas which is an inhaled agent
best_explanation: Lignocaine is a sodium channel blocker, so it inhibits the fast-gated sodium channels that are activated by voltagegated Na+ channels.  Nitrous oxide is a voltage gated Na+ channel blocker that works in a different way to local anaesthetics. It is used as a pre-medication to reduce anxiety and increase analgesia.  The other 3 options are central nervous system depressants and work by different mechanisms.  Diazepam is a voltage gated Na+ channel blocker and a benzodiazepine receptor agonist.  Propofol is a voltage gated Na+ channel blocker and acts as a GABA receptor agonist.  Amobarbital is a voltage gated Na+ channel blocker and a GABA receptor agonist.  Note that there are different types of local anaesthetic and different mechanisms of action.  This was covered in the "Nociception and Pain" lecture in Case 6. input: Given question: Which are the three muscles of the forearm that flex the wrist? reference: remember the rule of 3s'• 3 wrist flexors (flexor carpi radialis, flexor carpi ulnaris, palmaris longus)• 3 finger flexors (flexor digitorum superficialis, flexor digitorum profundus, flexor pollicis longus)• 3 wrist extensors (extensor carpi radialis longus, extensor carpi radialis brevis, extensor carpi ulnaris)• 3 finger extensors (extensor digitorum, extensor indicis, extensor digiti minimi)• 3 thumb extensors (abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis, extensor pollicis longus)

They are innervated by the median nerve and are supplied with blood by the radial artery.  The flexor carpi radialis muscle originates from the medial epicondyle of the humerus. The flexor carpi ulnaris muscle originates from the medial epicondyle of the humerus. The palmaris longus muscle originates from the centre of the anterior ridge of the humerus. instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: Upon fertilisation what hormone is produced by a developing embryo prior to placenta formation? Option A: Progesterone Option B: Oestrogen Option C: hCG Option D: GNRH The correct answer is Option C.
reference: A&B - Oestrogen and Progesterone are produced by the Corpus LuteumC - hCG is produced by the embryo to sustain the Corpus Luteum until the Placenta is formedD - Released by the Hypothalamus and activates the release of LH & FSH from the Anterior Pituitary Gland hCG is commonly used in pregnancy tests.
best_explanation: After fertilisation, the blastocyst releases hormones to ensure the endometrium remains receptive to implantation.  Prior to the development of the placenta, hCG is secreted.  Oestrogen and progesterone are secreted after the placenta has developed.  GNRH is released by the hypothalamus in response to low progesterone and oestrogen.  It stimulates the anterior pituitary to secrete the gonadotropins FSH and LH.  FSH and LH cause primary follicle development and therefore GnRH is involved in the initiation of the menstrual cycle.  In IVF, when there are no developing follicles, hCG is used to induce the development of the follicles (GnRH would have normally done this).  hCG can also be used to ensure the corpus luteum remains alive during the early stages of pregnancy, as it secretes progesterone. Progesterone is needed to maintain the endometrium and therefore a healthy environment for the developing embryo.  Oestrogen is also secreted by the corpus luteum, and is responsible for positive feedback of GnRH, which in turn causes more oestrogen and progesterone to be released.  As the placenta develops, it takes over the role of producing hormones from the corpus luteum.  Low progesterone and oestrogen cause GnRH to be released, which initiates the menstrual cycle. input: Given question: You are well into your shift at the A&E department, You have requested a blood gas on one of the patients and the results show that their partial pressure of oxygen is less than 8KPa, but their partial pressure of carbon dioxide is normal. You suspected type 1 respiratory failure and began treatment with oxygen and go on your way. A few hours later you return to see that the oxygen treatment isnt working and the patient is showing no signs of improvement. What was the cause of his respiratory failure? Option A: Low PiO2 Option B: VQ mismatch Option C: Pulmonary shunt Option D: diffusion impairment Option E: hypoventilation. The correct answer is Option C.
reference: This was in the case 5 lecture on respiratory failure.  Is somebody has respiratory failure first you need to consider which type it is. - Type 1: Oxygenation failure: the partial pressure of oxygen will be below 8Ka but the partial pressure of carbon dioxide will be normal or slightly below. there will be an increase a-A gradient.  - Type 2: Ventilation failure: the partial pressure of oxygen is below 8KPa but the partial pressure of carbon dioxide is above 6KPa. there is a normal a-A gradient.  knowing the type, you can then work out the treatment.- Type 1: treat with oxygen (there will be no improvement if the failure was caused by a pulmonary shunt)- Type 2: treat with non-invasive ventilation
best_explanation: This patient is suffering from a pulmonary shunt, as the blood gas results show that their partial pressure of oxygen is less than 8KPa, which is the normal value for the alveoli, but their partial pressure of carbon dioxide is normal, showing that the carbon dioxide is not being absorbed in the blood in the lung, so it must be passing into the venous system and going to the right side of the heart and then being vented to the atmosphere through the pulmonary arterial blood, bypassing the alveoli. This would mean that the patient would not be responding to oxygen treatment as the oxygen is not getting to the areas where it is needed. To treat this you would need to insert a bronchoscope into the lungs to find the site of the shunt and then place a catheter in the pulmonary artery to directly measure the shunt fraction.
